passages.title: The Wrong Shoes
text: On the morning of the school excursion, I put on my shoes in the dark and ran for the bus.
It was only when I sat down that I looked at my feet.
One shoe was mine. The other belonged to my brother, who is two years younger and two sizes smaller.
My left foot was already beginning to hurt.
I did not tell anybody. I was afraid the teachers would send me home, and we were going to the bird park, which I had waited three weeks for.
For the first hour I walked normally and pretended nothing was wrong. By the time we reached the flamingos I was limping.
Nur noticed first. She did not laugh. She asked what was wrong, and when I showed her, she went very quiet and thought for a while.
Then she took off her own shoes and handed me the left one.
"We wear the same size," she said. "I will wear your brother's."
Nur's feet are smaller than mine. My brother's shoe was far too tight for her, and I knew it.
She wore it for the rest of the day and said nothing at all about it.
On the bus home she took it off and I saw the red mark across her toes.
I have thought about that mark many times since. She was not being kind for one minute, which is easy. She was being kind for five hours, which is not.

questions.q: Why did the narrator put on the wrong shoes?
questions.a: He put them on in the dark, in a hurry to catch the bus for the excursion.
questions.tip: Look at the very first sentence.

questions.q: How were the two shoes different?
questions.a: One was his own. The other belonged to his younger brother, and was two sizes smaller.
questions.tip: Two details are needed: whose it was, and how much smaller.

questions.q: Why did the narrator not tell anybody?
questions.a: He was afraid the teachers would send him home, and he had been looking forward to the bird park for three weeks.
questions.tip: There are two reasons in the same sentence.

questions.q: How do we know the narrator's foot was getting worse?
questions.a: At first he walked normally and pretended nothing was wrong, but by the time they reached the flamingos he was limping.
questions.tip: Compare the first hour with later in the day.

questions.q: What did Nur do when she found out?
questions.a: She took off her own shoes and gave him her left one, and wore his brother's small shoe instead.
questions.tip: Say what she gave and what she took.

questions.q: Why was Nur's offer a bigger sacrifice than it first seems?
questions.a: Her feet were smaller than his, so his brother's shoe was far too tight for her, and she wore it for the rest of the day without complaining.
questions.tip: Think about whose foot the small shoe fitted worst.

questions.q: Which word in the passage means 'walking unevenly because of pain'?
questions.a: 'Limping'.
questions.tip: Look in the paragraph about the flamingos.

questions.q: How did the narrator find out how much it had hurt her?
questions.a: On the bus home she took the shoe off and he saw a red mark across her toes.
questions.tip: He saw it rather than being told.

questions.q: Explain the last sentence in your own words.
questions.a: Being kind for a short moment is easy because it costs you almost nothing. Nur stayed uncomfortable for five hours without mentioning it, and choosing to keep going is much harder than starting.
questions.tip: Contrast one minute with five hours, and say why the difference matters.

passages.title: Why We Queue
text: Queuing is not natural. It has to be learnt, and different places learn it differently.

In Singapore, a queue at a bus stop forms almost without discussion. People arrive, look, and place themselves at the end. Nobody appoints anybody. There is no line painted on the ground, and no official watching.
What holds it together is not a rule but an agreement, and agreements are fragile in a particular way: they work completely until they do not work at all.

Researchers who study queues have found that a single person stepping in near the front rarely causes an argument. Instead, something quieter happens. The people behind exchange glances. Bags are shifted. Somebody clears their throat. Very often the person who pushed in retreats without a single word being said to them.
This is remarkably efficient. A rule needs an inspector, a penalty and somebody to collect it. Social disapproval needs nothing at all, and it arrives instantly.

It is also fragile. In the same studies, once two or three people pushed in and nothing happened, the queue collapsed within a minute. Those who had been waiting patiently stopped waiting, because the cost of being patient had suddenly become obvious and the benefit had disappeared.

Not every culture queues the same way. In some places a crowd at a counter is the norm, and what looks like disorder to a visitor is a system with its own rules about who is served next. Neither arrangement is naturally better. What matters is that everybody in the room has learnt the same one, which is why the most difficult queues in the world are at international airports.

This is why queue systems in busy places increasingly use numbered tickets. A ticket does not make people more honest. It makes honesty unnecessary, which is a different thing and, in a crowded clinic on a Monday morning, a more reliable one.

There is one exception worth noticing. People are far more willing to let somebody go ahead of them when a reason is given, even a thin one. In one well-known experiment, asking to skip a photocopier queue succeeded far more often when the request ended with the word 'because', regardless of what followed it.
That finding is usually presented as evidence that people are easily fooled. It might equally show something better: that most of us would rather be reasonable than be first.

questions.q: According to the passage, what makes a queue at a bus stop work?
questions.a: Not an official rule, but an unspoken agreement between the people in it. Nobody appoints anybody and nobody is watching.
questions.tip: The answer is a contrast between two kinds of authority.

questions.q: Give two of the ways the passage says people react to somebody pushing in.
questions.a: Any two of: they exchange glances; they shift their bags; somebody clears their throat.
questions.tip: Three are listed; two will do.

questions.q: Why does the writer call social disapproval 'remarkably efficient'?
questions.a: Because a rule needs an inspector, a penalty and somebody to collect it, whereas disapproval costs nothing and works instantly.
questions.tip: The comparison with a formal rule is the point.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why a queue can collapse so quickly.
questions.a: Once a few people push in and nothing happens to them, waiting patiently starts to look pointless. The people who were waiting can now see that it costs them something and gains them nothing, so they stop.
questions.tip: Use the ideas of cost and benefit in your own words.

questions.q: What does the writer mean by saying a ticket 'makes honesty unnecessary'?
questions.a: A numbered ticket does not persuade anybody to behave better. It removes the need to rely on good behaviour at all, because your place is recorded rather than trusted.
questions.tip: Notice the difference between making people honest and not needing them to be.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention a clinic on a Monday morning?
questions.a: It is an example of a busy, crowded place where a queue depending on goodwill would be most likely to break down, so a ticket system is more reliable there.
questions.tip: Ask why that particular example was chosen.

questions.q: What did the photocopier experiment find?
questions.a: People were far more likely to let somebody skip the queue when the request included the word 'because', whatever reason followed it.
questions.tip: The key detail is that the reason itself did not matter.

questions.q: Which word in the passage means 'easily broken'?
questions.a: 'Fragile'.
questions.tip: It is used twice, about agreements and about the system.

questions.q: The writer offers two ways of reading the photocopier finding. What are they, and which does the writer prefer?
questions.a: It can be read as evidence that people are easily fooled by any reason at all. The writer prefers the second reading: that most people would rather behave reasonably than get to the front, so a reason gives them permission to be generous. The phrase 'It might equally show something better' shows the preference.
questions.tip: Give both readings, then quote or point to the words that show the writer's own view.

passages.title: The Cat That Came to School
text: The cat first appeared outside our classroom in the second week of January.

It was grey, thin, and missing part of one ear. It sat on the ledge outside the window during Mathematics and left before recess, and it did this every day for a fortnight before anybody mentioned it out loud.
Mr Devan pretended not to notice. We pretended not to notice that he was pretending.
Then somebody brought food.
It was Wei Ling, and she brought half a sausage from her lunchbox, and after that the cat stayed until the end of the day.
Within a week, four people were bringing food. The cat grew visibly rounder. It also began to walk into the classroom.
That was when Mr Devan stopped pretending.
He did not shout. He asked us to sit down, and then he asked one question: what would happen to the cat in March, when we moved to a different block?
Nobody had thought about March.
He explained that a cat fed by children learns to expect children, and that a cat which has learnt to expect children and then finds none is in a worse position than a cat that never learnt anything.
We argued for twenty minutes. Some of us were angry, mostly because he was right.

In the end we did something better than feeding it. Wei Ling's mother knew somebody at a rescue centre. They came on a Thursday, caught it in about four minutes, and took it away to be checked and rehomed.
We were sent a photograph in April. It lives with an elderly couple in Bedok and has become extremely fat.
I still look at the window ledge sometimes during Mathematics. It is the right ending, and I know that, and I still look.

questions.q: How long had the cat been visiting before anybody spoke about it?
questions.a: A fortnight, which is two weeks.
questions.tip: The passage gives the length in the second paragraph.

questions.q: Give two details that describe how the cat looked when it first appeared.
questions.a: Any two of: it was grey; it was thin; part of one ear was missing.
questions.tip: Three details are given; two will do.

questions.q: What does 'We pretended not to notice that he was pretending' tell us about the class?
questions.a: They knew Mr Devan had seen the cat and was deliberately ignoring it, and they were happy to play along so that nothing would have to be done about it.
questions.tip: Both the teacher and the class are choosing not to act.

questions.q: What changed after Wei Ling brought food?
questions.a: The cat began staying until the end of the day, four people started bringing food, it grew visibly rounder, and it began coming into the classroom.
questions.tip: Several things changed; give at least two.

questions.q: What was Mr Devan's argument against feeding the cat?
questions.a: A cat fed by children learns to expect children. When the class moved block in March there would be no children, and a cat that has learnt to expect food and then finds none is worse off than one that never learnt to expect it.
questions.tip: His argument is about what happens after the feeding stops.

questions.q: Why were some pupils angry?
questions.a: Mostly because he was right, and they could not argue against it.
questions.tip: The passage says so directly.

questions.q: Why does the writer say what they did in the end was 'better than feeding it'?
questions.a: Feeding the cat only helped while they were there. Having it caught, checked and rehomed gave it a permanent home, which solves the problem instead of postponing it.
questions.tip: Compare a short-term help with a lasting one.

questions.q: Which word in the passage means 'given a new home'?
questions.a: 'Rehomed'.
questions.tip: Look in the paragraph about the rescue centre.

questions.q: Explain the last sentence: 'It is the right ending, and I know that, and I still look.'
questions.a: The narrator accepts that rehoming the cat was the right decision and does not regret it. Even so, he misses it, and the habit of looking at the ledge has stayed with him. Knowing something is right does not stop you feeling the loss of it.
questions.tip: The sentence holds two things at once. Say what both are.

passages.title: The Understudy's Understudy
text: There were three of us who could play the part, and I was the third.
Pei Shan had it. Hafiz was her understudy, which meant he learnt every line and would go on only if she could not. I was Hafiz's understudy, which meant almost nothing at all.
Mrs Fong was honest about it. "You will not perform," she told me in September. "Two people would both have to be ill. It has happened to me once in twenty-two years."
I learnt the part anyway. I am not sure why. Possibly because being told something is nearly impossible is not quite the same as being told it is impossible.
I went to every rehearsal. I sat at the side with the script on my knees and mouthed the lines while Pei Shan spoke them. For eleven weeks I was the least important person in the hall.
What I did not expect was how much I would learn there.

Because I was never on stage, I watched. I saw Mrs Fong ask Pei Shan to say one line six times, and I understood on the fourth attempt what she was listening for. I saw Hafiz solve a problem with a difficult entrance by changing where he stood two lines earlier. Nobody explained these things to me. I simply had nothing else to do but notice them.

There was one afternoon in week nine when Pei Shan lost her voice and could not rehearse. Hafiz went on in her place, and Mrs Fong turned to me and said, "You are Hafiz today." I sat in his chair at the side of the hall for two hours, holding his script, and did not speak a single line. It was the closest I came all term, and it lasted one afternoon.
On the night, Pei Shan was not ill and neither was Hafiz. I watched from the third row with my parents.
She was very good. He would have been very good. I would have been adequate, and I knew it, because I had spent eleven weeks watching people who were better than me.
That is the part nobody warned me about, and it is the part I am most grateful for.
In March I auditioned for the next production and got a speaking part. Mrs Fong said something afterwards that I have kept.
"You were the only one who had already been to every rehearsal."

questions.q: Explain what an understudy is, using the passage.
questions.a: Somebody who learns every line of a part and performs it only if the person who has the part cannot.
questions.tip: The passage explains it when Hafiz is introduced.

questions.q: Why did the narrator's position mean 'almost nothing at all'?
questions.a: He was the understudy's understudy, so two people would both have had to be unable to perform before he would go on.
questions.tip: The reason is arithmetical.

questions.q: What did Mrs Fong tell the narrator in September, and why is her exact wording important?
questions.a: She said he would not perform, because it would take two people being ill, which had happened once in twenty-two years. The wording matters because she said it was nearly impossible rather than impossible, and the narrator notices that difference and learns the part anyway.
questions.tip: Give what she said and then explain what the narrator makes of it.

questions.q: Give two things the narrator learnt by watching rather than performing.
questions.a: Any two of: he understood what Mrs Fong was listening for when she made Pei Shan repeat a line; he saw how Hafiz fixed a difficult entrance by changing where he stood two lines earlier.
questions.tip: Two examples are given in the same paragraph.

questions.q: Why was the narrator able to notice these things?
questions.a: Because he was never on stage he had nothing else to do but watch, so he had time to see things nobody explained to him.
questions.tip: The reason is about what he was not doing.

questions.q: What happened on the night of the performance?
questions.a: Neither Pei Shan nor Hafiz was ill, so the narrator did not perform. He watched from the third row with his parents.
questions.tip: The outcome is plainly stated.

questions.q: Why does the narrator say he would have been only 'adequate'?
questions.a: Because he had spent eleven weeks watching two people who were better than he was, so he could judge his own level honestly.
questions.tip: He gives the reason in the same sentence.

questions.q: Which word in the passage means 'good enough, but no better'?
questions.a: 'Adequate'.
questions.tip: It is used about himself, not about the others.

questions.q: Why is Mrs Fong's last remark a good ending to the story?
questions.a: It shows that the eleven weeks were not wasted after all. The thing that got him a speaking part was exactly the thing that had seemed pointless: turning up to every rehearsal when he had no chance of performing. It rewards the narrator without pretending he was talented, which is more honest and more satisfying.
questions.tip: Connect her remark back to the weeks that seemed to be for nothing.
